paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Koalas are just too nice for their own good. Except for the occasional baby taken by birds of prey, koalas have no natural enemies. In an ideal world, the life of an arboreal couch potato would be perfectly safe and acceptable.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Just two hundred years ago, koalas flourished across Australia. Now they seem to be in decline, but exact numbers are not available because the species does not appear to be ‘under threat’. Their problem, however, has been human activity, particularly since European settlement. Koalas and Aboriginal Australians had coexisted peacefully for centuries.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Today koalas are found only in scattered pockets of southeast Australia, where they seem to be at risk on several fronts. The koala’s only food source, the eucalyptus tree, has become less abundant. In the past 200 years, a third of Australia’s eucalyptus forests have disappeared. Koalas have been killed by parasites, chlamydia epidemics and a tumour-causing retro-virus. And every year 11,000 are killed by cars, ironically most of them in wildlife sanctuaries, and thousands are killed by poachers. Some are also taken illegally as pets. The animals usually die soon, but poachers can easily replace them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Bushfires pose another threat. The horrific ones that raged in New South Wales recently killed between 100 and 1,000 koalas. Many that were taken into sanctuaries and shelters were found to have burnt their paws on the glowing embers. But zoologists say that the species should recover. The koalas will be aided by the eucalyptus, which grows quickly and is already regenerating after the fires. So the main threat to their survival is their slow reproductive rate – they produce only one baby a year over a reproductive lifespan of about nine years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The latest problem for the species is perhaps more insidious. With plush, grey fur, dark amber eyes and button nose, koalas are the very image of cuddliness. Australian zoos and wildlife parks have taken advantage of their uncomplaining attitudes, and charge visitors to be photographed hugging the furry bundles. People may not realise how cruel this is: because of the koala’s delicate disposition, constant handling can push their already precariously balanced physiology beyond its limits.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Koalas eat between 600 and 1,250 grams of foliage from certain eucalyptus species each day. The tough leaves are packed with cellulose, tannins, aromatic oils and precursors of toxic cyanides. To handle this cocktail, koalas have a specialised digestive system. Cellulose-digesting bacteria in the caecum break down fibre, while a specially adapted gut and liver process the toxins. To digest their food properly, koalas must sit still for 21 hours every day.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Koalas are the epitome of innocence and inoffensiveness. Although they are capable of ripping open a person’s arm with their needle-sharp claws or delivering a nasty bite, they simply do not attack. If you upset a koala, it may blink or swallow, or hiccup. But attack? No way! Koalas are just not aggressive. They use their claws to grip the hard smooth bark of eucalyptus trees.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: They are also very sensitive, and the slightest upset can prevent them from breeding, cause them to go off their food and make them susceptible to gut infections. Koalas are stoic creatures and put on a brave face until they are at death’s door. One day they may appear healthy; the next, they could be dead. Captive koalas have to be weighed daily to check that they are feeding properly. A sudden loss of weight is usually the only warning keepers have that their charge is ill. Only two keepers plus a vet were allowed to handle London Zoo’s koalas, as these creatures are only comfortable with people they know. A request for the koala to be taken to meet the Queen was refused because of the distress this would have caused the marsupial. Sadly, London Zoo no longer has a koala. Two years ago the female koala died of a cancer caused by a retrovirus. When they come into heat, female koalas become more active, and start losing weight, but after about sixteen days, oestrus ends and the weight piles back on. London’s koala did not. Surgery revealed hundreds of pea-sized tumours.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Almost every zoo in Australia has koalas—the marsupial has become the Animal Ambassador of the nation—but nowhere outside Australia would handling by the public be allowed. Koala cuddling flies in the face of every rule of good care. First, some zoos allow koalas to be passed from stranger to stranger, including many children who love to squeeze them. Secondly, most people have no idea how to handle the animals; koalas like to cling to their handler, in their own time, and use his or her arm as a tree. For these reasons, the Association of Fauna and Marine Parks, an Australian conservation society, is campaigning to ban koala cuddling. Policy on koala handling is determined by state government authorities. The association is also lobbying the Australian Nature Conservation Agency, with the aim of establishing national guidelines. Following a wave of publicity, some zoos and wildlife parks have stopped using their koalas as photographic props.

questionGroups.text:
Questions 14–18
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write your answers in boxes 14–18 on your answer sheet.


14 Koala numbers have declined for all the following reasons EXCEPT
 A poaching.
 B disease.
 C frequent births from which few offspring survive.
 D road accidents.


15 What helps koalas fully digest their food?
 A toxic substances in the leaves.
 B organs that dissolve fibre.
 C remaining inactive for a long period.
 D eating eucalyptus leaves.


16 How do koalas react when threatened?
 A They show signs of distress.
 B They counterattack furiously.
 C They use their sharp claws to injure people.
 D They use their claws to grip tree bark.


17 How do Australian zoos exploit koalas?
 A They encourage people to breed koalas as pets.
 B They allow tourists to hug koalas.
 C They place koalas in trees as symbols.
 D They establish koala campaigns.

18 What may the authorities do to protect koalas?
 A Introduce national guidelines for handling koalas.
 B Close some zoos.
 C Discourage the public from visiting zoos.
 D Persuade the public to learn more about koalas.

Questions 19–25
Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 2?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN in boxes 19–25 on your answer sheet.
 YES                         if the statement agrees with the views of the writer

 NO                          if the statement contradicts the views of the writer

 NOT GIVEN                   if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this


19 Newly arrived human settlers posed a danger to koalas.
20 Koalas can still be seen throughout most of Australia.
21 It takes decades for eucalyptus trees to recover after a fire.
22 Koalas fight one another when food becomes scarce.
23 It is difficult to notice when koalas are ill.
24 Koalas easily contract contagious human diseases through cuddling.
25 Koalas like to hold a person’s arm when they are embraced.

Question 26
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write your answer in box 26 on your answer sheet.


26 In your opinion, this article was written by
  A a journalist writing for a magazine.
  B a keeper at London Zoo.
  C a tourist returning from Australia.
  D a government official studying koalas to draft legislation.
